content: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is an autoimmune disorder that disrupts neuromuscular transmission. Treatments for LEMS aim to either counteract the autoimmune process or enhance the remaining neuromuscular transmission. To evaluate the effectiveness of treatments for LEMS, a systematic review was conducted. The search included databases such as the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies up to October 2010. The review focused on randomized or quasi-randomized trials involving adults and children diagnosed with LEMS, with or without associated small-cell lung cancer, who received any pharmacological or physical treatment. Four controlled trials involving 3,4-diaminopyridine (3,4-DAP) were identified, including three cross-over trials and one parallel-group trial, with a total of 54 participants. Two of these trials were newly added in the updated review. One trial also evaluated the combination of 3,4-DAP with pyridostigmine. Additionally, a separate cross-over trial compared intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) to placebo in nine participants. The trials involving 3,4-DAP demonstrated significant improvements in muscle strength scores and myometric limb measurements within hours to a week after treatment. There was also a significant increase in resting compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitude compared to placebo. A meta-analysis of the primary endpoint, the Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis (QMG) muscle score, showed an average improvement of 2.44 points (95% confidence interval: 1.22 to 3.6) between three and eight days of treatment. For the secondary endpoint, CMAP amplitude, the meta-analysis revealed a mean improvement of 1.36 mV (95% confidence interval: 0.99 to 1.72) over the same period. The risk of bias in these studies was considered low, and the quality of evidence was rated as moderate to high. The single cross-over trial evaluating IVIg reported significant improvements in myometric limb strength and a non-significant increase in mean resting CMAP amplitude compared to placebo. Clinical benefits from IVIg were observed to last up to eight weeks. In conclusion, limited but moderate to high-quality evidence from randomized controlled trials indicates that 3,4-DAP improves muscle strength scores and CMAP amplitudes over a period of days, while IVIg provides clinical improvement for up to eight weeks in individuals with LEMS. However, there is currently insufficient data to quantify the effects of these treatments fully, and other potential therapies have not yet been evaluated in randomized controlled trials.
